observations.text: Main article reports random assignment to extended-release exenatide 2 mg or matching placebo weekly; defines primary composite first occurrence of cardiovascular death, nonfatal MI, or nonfatal stroke; reports coprimary noninferiority/superiority hypotheses; and identifies EXSCEL as NCT01144338.
Participants were randomly assigned 1:1; the report describes computer-generated block randomization within each site, stratified by cardiovascular history.
Primary endpoint is first occurrence of cardiovascular death, nonfatal MI, or nonfatal stroke in a time-to-event analysis.
Primary time-to-event analyses used Cox proportional hazards in ITT, defined as all randomized patients.
Primary ITT result: HR 0.91 (95% CI 0.83 to 1.00), noninferior for safety, not superior for efficacy.
Main article names EXSCEL ClinicalTrials.gov number NCT01144338; intake condition records registry query NCT01455896 unavailable. Identifier conflict is unresolved; no registry obtained.

interpretations.text: The source-reported Result matches the requested endpoint event set, time-to-first-event, ITT population, comparison, and primary HR.

result.relation_rationale: The selected primary report explicitly defines its primary composite as the first occurrence of cardiovascular death, nonfatal MI, or nonfatal stroke, analyzed time-to-event. This matches the requested component set and first-event estimand during trial follow-up. Its primary ITT comparison is extended-release exenatide 2 mg weekly versus matching placebo, reported as HR 0.91 (95% CI 0.83 to 1.00); the coprimary hypotheses were noninferiority for safety and superiority for efficacy. The article identifies EXSCEL as NCT01144338, while captured intake metadata declares NCT01455896. Registry retrieval was unavailable, so applicability to the conflicting intake identifier remains unresolved; I do not silently reconcile these identifiers.

questions.official_guidance: Answer ‘Yes’ if a random component was used in the sequence generation process. Examples include computer-generated random numbers; reference to a random number table; coin tossing; shuffling cards or envelopes; throwing dice; or drawing lots. Answer ‘No’ if no random element was used in generating the allocation sequence or the sequence is predictable. Answer ‘No information’ if the only information about randomization methods is a statement that the study is randomized.
questions.source_locator: Full guidance p. 17, Box 4, signalling question 1.1
questions.bias_construct: Whether a random component was used to generate the allocation sequence.
questions.decision_rule: Answer yes when a random component was used; answer no when no random element was used or the sequence is predictable. A statement that the study is randomized alone supports no_information.
evidence_needed: The sequence-generation method, such as computer random numbers, a random number table, coin tossing, or minimization with a random element.
questions.no_information_rule: Answer no_information when the only information about randomization methods is that the study is randomized. Do not turn missing reporting into proof that the sequence was non-random.

answer_anchors.text: A random component was used in sequence generation.
No random element was used, or the sequence was predictable.
The report only states that the study is randomized.

considerations: Minimization should generally be considered random when it includes a random element.

Sequence generation asks how the allocation sequence was produced; concealment asks whether forthcoming assignments were hidden before enrolment and assignment; baseline imbalance asks whether the resulting groups suggest a randomization problem. Evidence for one does not answer the others.
The baseline-imbalance answer must not change this answer.
Use the returned query suggestions or wording from the report to locate the sequence method. A truncated search does not establish that the method is absent.

use of open-label glucose-lowering agents (includ-

receptor agonists) was encouraged to promote
glycemic equipoise between the two trial groups
and to help patients reach clinically appropriate
glycated hemoglobin targets.
Outcomes
The primary outcome was defined as the first
occurrence of any component of the composite
outcome of death from cardiovascular causes,
nonfatal myocardial infarction, or nonfatal stroke
(three-component MACE outcome), in a time-to-
event analysis. Secondary outcomes included
death from any cause, death from cardiovascular
causes, and the first occurrence of nonfatal or
fatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal or fatal
stroke, hospitalization for acute coronary syn-
drome, and hospitalization for heart failure, in
time-to-event analyses. An independent clinical
events classification committee whose members
were unaware of the trial-group assignments ad-
judicated all the components of the primary com-
posite outcome, secondary outcomes, ventricular
arrhythmias that led to intervention, neoplasms,
and pancreatitis; these events are defined in the
Clinical Event Definitions section in the Supple-
mentary Appendix.
Additional outcomes that were prespecified
in the protocol included a composite of death
from cardiovascular causes or hospitalization for
heart failure, the first confirmed revasculariza-
tion procedure, initiation of the first interven-
tional glucose-lowering medication received dur-
ing the trial other than the trial regimen, and
absolute values and changes from baseline in
glycated hemoglobin level, body weight, blood
pressure, and lipid levels. Prespecified events of
clinical interest for which information was col-
lected systematically at every follow-up visit,
regardless of seriousness, were pancreatitis, neo-
plasm, severe hypoglycemia, and expected car-
diovascular or diabetes-related complications.
Information on other nonserious adverse events
was not collected (details are provided in Section
10.3 in the protocol).
Patients were followed for adverse events un-
til the end of the trial or 70 days after discon-
tinuation of the trial regimen. For patients who
were either lost to follow-up or had withdrawn
consent, vital status was ascertained during the
70-day washout period by searches conducted
with the use of local or national electronic
health records, death registries, or other publicly
available sources (as permitted by local ethics
approvals).

guidance: Answer every initially active question plus each dependent question whose activation predicate is met by your earlier answers. Extra inactive branch answers are ignored and never committed. Preserve the approved Result target.

Evaluate activated questions in question order. Submit every activated question with a justification, unknowns, and counterevidence. Review the inspected passages against its exact proposition and check material contradictions. Reuse adequate Evidence. When a premise remains unresolved, state the unresolved premise and why you stopped, and use bounded discovery across relevant Sources, including a protocol or SAP when relevant. Inspect returned passages before using them. A limitation requires that explicit premise and stopping rationale; include a Trial-scoped search receipt when retrieval provenance is useful, but a direct read does not require a search receipt. Absence requires a scoped untruncated no-hit receipt.

Cite complete premises for the active question. One passage may support several facts. When an answer depends on separate passages, cite each with its own boundaries. A relationship kind describes the use of Evidence; it adds no scientific fact.

When inference, conflict, or uncertainty connects Evidence to an answer, include a concise question-specific justification. State what the passages establish, what remains unresolved, and why the selected option follows. Any support relationship is host-asserted: the server checks structure, ownership, and exact Evidence provenance but does not independently judge semantic entailment.

Working premise records are source-grounded resumable notes. Reuse them only when the working checkpoint is current for this exact approved Result and captured Source projection; a stale checkpoint requires the stated recovery action and never carries a prior Domain judgment into this assessment.

A definitive yes or no needs direct_support, indirect_support, or contradiction; a limitation or absence alone supports uncertainty, not a definitive answer. For D3.2 No, inspected context/inference or a valid scoped no-hit receipt can instead support the scoped absence of reassuring evidence; it does not assert bias occurred.

Evaluate activation against your draft answers. If validation reports missing active question IDs, add those questions with allowed answer values and supported bases, then resubmit the complete active set in one validation call. The server commits only active answers.

Apply every reported repair and retain other drafted answers. Add missing questions to the existing answer set. Resolve further activation from the repaired answers before resubmitting. The server ignores inactive answers.

response_framework.firm_evidence_rule: The definitive versions (‘Yes’ and ‘No’) would typically imply that firm evidence is available in relation to the signalling question.
response_framework.probable_judgment_rule: The ‘Probably’ versions would typically imply that a judgement has been made. ‘Yes’ and ‘Probably yes’ have the same implications for risk of bias, as do ‘No’ and ‘Probably no’.
response_framework.no_information_rule: Use ‘No information’ only when both (i) insufficient details are reported to permit a response of ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’, and (ii) in the absence of these details it would be unreasonable to respond ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’ in the circumstances of the trial.
response_framework.independence_rule: Signalling questions should be answered independently: the answer to one question should not affect answers to other questions in the same or other domains other than through determining which subsequent questions are answered.
response_framework.quotation_rule: Brief direct quotations from the text of the study report should be used whenever possible to support the answer.

traps: A no-hit search describes one lexical query, not scientific absence.
A planned method does not prove conduct; a time origin or analysis population does not prove complete follow-up or equal assessment.
An endpoint label or definition does not prove objectivity, blinding, prespecification, or no alternative analyses.
A treatment assignment or visibly different intervention does not by itself prove that participants or personnel knew the assignment.
Different treatment or visit schedules do not by themselves prove that outcome measurement differed between groups.
Stratification does not prove allocation concealment.
data.completion_rule: Ground each active proposition and uncertainty in inspected Evidence, scoped search receipts, or an explicit scientific limitation. Complete reading_recovery with read_pages and all context continuations. Document-structure recovery in coverage is navigation, not selected Evidence; inspect relevant unopened windows before claiming information is unreported, or retain a bounded stopping rationale. Inactive extras are ignored.

Answer ‘Yes’ if envelopes or drug containers were used appropriately. Answer ‘No’ if there is reason to suspect that the enrolling investigator or the participant had knowledge of the forthcoming allocation.

sections.excerpt: Note that differences that are compatible with chance do not lead to a risk of bias. Answer ‘No’ if no imbalances are apparent or if any observed imbalances are compatible with chance. Answer ‘Yes’ if there are imbalances that indicate problems with the randomization process, including substantial differences between intervention group sizes, a substantial excess in statistically significant differences beyond that expected by chance, or imbalance in one or more key prognostic factors very unlikely to be due to chance. Answer ‘No information’ when there is no useful baseline information available.

21|BACKGROUND
22|The cardiovascular effects of adding once-weekly treatment with exenatide to usual
23|care in patients with type 2 diabetes are unknown.
24|METHODS
25|We randomly assigned patients with type 2 diabetes, with or without previous car-
26|diovascular disease, to receive subcutaneous injections of extended-release exenatide
27|at a dose of 2 mg or matching placebo once weekly. The primary composite out-
28|come was the first occurrence of death from cardiovascular causes, nonfatal myo-
29|cardial infarction, or nonfatal stroke. The coprimary hypotheses were that exena-
30|tide, administered once weekly, would be noninferior to placebo with respect to
31|safety and superior to placebo with respect to efficacy.
32|RESULTS
33|In all, 14,752 patients (of whom 10,782 [73.1%] had previous cardiovascular
34|disease) were followed for a median of 3.2 years (interquartile range, 2.2 to 4.4).
35|A primary composite outcome event occurred in 839 of 7356 patients (11.4%; 3.7
36|events per 100 person-years) in the exenatide group and in 905 of 7396 patients
37|(12.2%; 4.0 events per 100 person-years) in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.91;
38|95% confidence interval [CI], 0.83 to 1.00), with the intention-to-treat analysis
39|indicating that exenatide, administered once weekly, was noninferior to placebo with
40|respect to safety (P<0.001 for noninferiority) but was not superior to placebo
41|with respect to efficacy (P = 0.06 for superiority). The rates of death from cardio-
42|vascular causes, fatal or nonfatal myocardial infarction, fatal or nonfatal stroke,
43|hospitalization for heart failure, and hospitalization for acute coronary syndrome,
44|and the incidence of acute pancreatitis, pancreatic cancer, medullary thyroid
45|carcinoma, and serious adverse events did not differ significantly between the two
46|groups.
47|CONCLUSIONS
48|Among patients with type 2 diabetes with or without previous cardiovascular
49|disease, the incidence of major adverse cardiovascular events did not differ sig-
50|nificantly between patients who received exenatide and those who received pla-
51|cebo. (Funded by Amylin Pharmaceuticals; EXSCEL ClinicalTrials.gov number,
52|NCT01144338.)

4|T
5|he risk of death from any cause
6|among persons with type 2 diabetes is up
7|to twice that of the general population,1
8|and the risk of death from cardiovascular causes
9|is up to four times that of the general popula-
10|tion.2,3 Improved glycemic control has been shown
11|to improve microvascular outcomes,4,5 but a bene-
12|ficial effect on macrovascular outcomes is less
13|certain.6 In trials that assessed cardiovascular
14|outcomes associated with the use of newer glucose-
15|lowering agents, no effect on major adverse
16|cardiovascular events (MACE) was shown with
17|three dipeptidyl peptidase 4 (DPP-4) inhibitors
18|(saxagliptin, alogliptin, and sitagliptin)7-9 and one
19|exendin-4-based glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1)
20|receptor agonist (lixisenatide),10 but a lower risk
21|of MACE was shown with two GLP-1 receptor
22|agonists (liraglutide and semaglutide)11,12 and
23|two sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT-2)
24|inhibitors (empagliflozin and canagliflozin).13,14
25|A once-weekly, injectable, extended-release for-
26|mulation of exenatide, an exendin-4-based GLP-1
27|receptor agonist approved for the treatment of
28|type 2 diabetes, has been shown to lower blood
29|glucose and induce modest decreases in body
30|weight, blood pressure, and lipid levels15,16 but
31|has also been shown to increase heart rate.17,18
32|In accordance with regulatory guidance,19,20 the
33|Exenatide Study of Cardiovascular Event Lower-
34|ing (EXSCEL) assessed the long-term cardiovas-
35|cular safety and efficacy of exenatide, administered
36|once weekly, in patients with type 2 diabetes
37|who had a wide range of cardiovascular risk.
38|Methods
39|Trial Oversight
40|We conducted this pragmatic, randomized, double-
41|blind, placebo-controlled, event-driven trial at
42|687 sites in 35 countries. The design of this aca-
43|demically led trial has been reported previously.21
44|A diagram showing the overall design is provided
45|in Figure S1 in the Supplementary Appendix, avail-
46|able with the full text of this article at NEJM.org.
47|The trial was conducted jointly by the Duke
48|Clinical Research Institute and the University of
49|Oxford Diabetes Trials Unit in collaboration with
50|the sponsor, Amylin Pharmaceuticals, a wholly
51|owned subsidiary of AstraZeneca. The protocol,
52|which was approved by the ethics committee at
53|each participating site, and the statistical analy-
54|sis plan are available at NEJM.org. The statistical
55|analyses were performed by the Duke Clinical
56|Research Institute, independent of the sponsor.
57|Details of the trial organization and a complete
58|list of the investigators are provided in the Sup-
59|plementary Appendix.
60|All the patients provided written informed
61|consent. Our trial was designed and overseen by
62|a steering committee composed of nine investi-
63|gators and two employees of the sponsor. An
64|independent data and safety monitoring commit-
65|tee, who had access to unblinded data, performed
66|regular safety surveillance. All the authors had
67|access to the final trial results and vouch for the
68|accuracy and completeness of the data and
69|analyses and for the fidelity of the trial to the
70|protocol. The manuscript, drafted by the second
71|and third authors, was revised and approved by
72|all the authors, who assume responsibility for its
73|accuracy and completeness and made the deci-
74|sion to submit the manuscript for publication.
75|Trial Population
76|Adults with type 2 diabetes (defined as a glycated
77|hemoglobin level of 6.5 to 10.0% [48 to 96 mmol
78|per mole]) were eligible for participation in the
79|trial. The trial was designed such that approxi-
80|mately 70% of enrolled patients would have had
81|previous cardiovascular events and 30% would
82|not have had previous cardiovascular events.
83|Previous cardiovascular events were defined as a
84|history of major clinical manifestation of coro-
85|nary artery disease, ischemic cerebrovascular dis-
86|ease, or atherosclerotic peripheral arterial disease.
87|Patients were permitted to receive up to three
88|oral glucose-lowering agents or to receive insulin,
89|either alone or in combination with up to two
90|oral glucose-lowering agents. Key exclusion cri-
91|teria were a history of two or more episodes of
92|severe hypoglycemia (defined as hypoglycemia for
93|which a patient received third-party assistance)
94|during the preceding 12 months, end-stage kid-
95|ney disease or an estimated glomerular filtra-
96|tion rate (eGFR) at entry of less than 30 ml per
97|minute per 1.73 m2 of body-surface area, a per-
98|sonal or family history of medullary thyroid car-
99|cinoma or multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2,
100|a baseline calcitonin level of greater than 40 ng
101|per liter, or previous treatment with a GLP-1
102|receptor agonist.

49|and pancreatitis; these events are defined in the
50|Clinical Event Definitions section in the Supple-
51|mentary Appendix.
52|Additional outcomes that were prespecified
53|in the protocol included a composite of death
54|from cardiovascular causes or hospitalization for
55|heart failure, the first confirmed revasculariza-
56|tion procedure, initiation of the first interven-
57|tional glucose-lowering medication received dur-
58|ing the trial other than the trial regimen, and
59|absolute values and changes from baseline in
60|glycated hemoglobin level, body weight, blood
61|pressure, and lipid levels. Prespecified events of
62|clinical interest for which information was col-
63|lected systematically at every follow-up visit,
64|regardless of seriousness, were pancreatitis, neo-
65|plasm, severe hypoglycemia, and expected car-
66|diovascular or diabetes-related complications.
67|Information on other nonserious adverse events
68|was not collected (details are provided in Section
69|10.3 in the protocol).
70|Patients were followed for adverse events un-
71|til the end of the trial or 70 days after discon-
72|tinuation of the trial regimen. For patients who
73|were either lost to follow-up or had withdrawn
74|consent, vital status was ascertained during the
75|70-day washout period by searches conducted
76|with the use of local or national electronic
77|health records, death registries, or other publicly
78|available sources (as permitted by local ethics
79|approvals).
80|Statistical Analysis
81|Information on sample size and power calcula-
82|tions has been published previously 21; we esti-
83|mated that with 1360 patients with a confirmed
84|primary composite outcome event, the trial would
85|have 85% power to detect a risk of a primary
86|composite outcome event that was 15% lower
87|with once-weekly administration of exenatide
88|than with placebo, at a two-sided alpha level of
89|0.05. The time-to-event analyses were performed
90|with the use of a Cox proportional-hazards
91|model for primary, secondary, and exploratory
92|outcomes in the intention-to-treat population,
93|stratified according to history of cardiovascular
94|disease, with trial regimen as an explanatory
95|variable. The intention-to-treat population includ-
96|ed all patients who underwent randomization.
97|The Kaplan-Meier method was used to calculate
98|event rates. The primary safety hypothesis was
99|that exenatide, administered once weekly, would
100|be noninferior to placebo for the primary out-
101|come, with a noninferiority margin of 1.3 for the
102|upper limit of the two-sided 95% confidence
103|interval of the hazard ratio. The primary efficacy
104|hypothesis was that exenatide, administered once
105|weekly, would be superior to placebo, with a

7|of hierarchical testing in the following order:
8|noninferiority for the primary composite out-
9|come, superiority for the primary composite
10|outcome, superiority for all-cause mortality, supe-
11|riority for each component of the cardiovascular
12|composite (tested with the use of the Hochberg
13|procedure), and finally, if all three components
14|were superior, superiority for hospitalization for
15|acute coronary syndrome and for hospitalization
16|for heart failure (tested with the use of the Hoch
17|berg procedure). In accordance with the hierarchi-
18|cal testing plan, if a significant difference was
19|not found for an outcome, formal hypothesis
20|testing was not to be conducted for the remain-
21|ing ordered outcomes.
22|Sensitivity analyses of the primary efficacy
23|outcome were performed in the per-protocol
24|population, which included all randomized pa-
25|tients who received at least one dose of the trial
26|regimen and had no major protocol violations
27|(see the protocol for further details). The safety
28|analyses were performed in patients who under-
29|went randomization and received at least one
30|dose of exenatide or placebo.
31|Baseline characteristics were summarized as
32|means and standard deviations, medians and
33|interquartile ranges, or percentages. The primary
34|composite outcome was analyzed in prespecified
35|subgroups that were defined according to base-
36|line characteristics, including age at randomiza-
37|tion, sex, race, geographic region, type of glucose-
38|lowering therapy, duration of diabetes, history
39|or no history of a cardiovascular event or heart
40|failure, body-mass index, glycated hemoglobin
41|level, and kidney function. Repeated measures,
42|such as glycated hemoglobin level and body
43|weight, were analyzed with the use of longitudi-
44|nal models with mixed effects, with differences
45|between the trial groups estimated by least-
46|squares mean differences with 95% confidence
47|intervals. Analyses were conducted with the use
48|of SAS software, version 9.4 (SAS Institute).
49|Results
50|Trial Patients
51|In all, 14,752 patients (of whom 10,782 [73.1%]
52|had previous cardiovascular disease) underwent
53|randomization from June 18, 2010, through Sep-
54|tember 16, 2015, and were included in the inten-
55|tion-to-treat population; 7356 patients were as-
56|signed to receive exenatide and 7396 to receive
57|placebo once weekly (Fig. S2 in the Supplemen-
58|tary Appendix).22 The planned closeout of follow-
59|up of the patients was from December 5, 2016,
60|to May 11, 2017, after the prespecified required
61|minimum of 1360 patients were confirmed to
62|have had a primary composite outcome event.
63|The demographic, disease, and clinical char-
64|acteristics of the patients did not differ signifi-
65|cantly between the groups, nor did the use of
66|glucose-lowering agents or medications to reduce
67|the risk of cardiovascular disease, with the excep-
68|tion of lipid-lowering medications and SGLT-2
69|inhibitors (Table S1 in the Supplementary Ap-
70|pendix).22 At baseline, the median length of time
71|that patients had had diabetes was 12.0 years
72|(interquartile range, 7.0 to 18.0), the median
73|glycated hemoglobin level was 8.0% (interquar-
74|tile range, 7.3 to 8.9) (63.9 mmol per mole [inter-
75|quartile range, 56.3 to 73.8]), and 2389 patients
76|(16.2%) had a history of heart failure.
77|A total of 14,187 patients (96.2%) completed
78|the trial, and vital status was obtained for 98.8%
79|of the patients. The median duration of follow-
80|up was 3.2 years (interquartile range, 2.2 to 4.4;
81|maximum, 6.8) and was similar in the two
82|groups. The median duration of exposure to the
83|trial regimen was 2.4 years (interquartile range,
84|1.4 to 3.8) in the exenatide group and 2.3 years
85|(interquartile range, 1.2 to 3.6) in the placebo
86|group. The mean percentage of time that partici-
87|pants received the trial regimen (i.e., the dura-
88|tion of time that participants received the trial
89|regimen relative to the duration of time that they
90|were expected to receive the regimen during the
91|trial) was 76.0% and 75.0%, respectively. Prema-
92|ture discontinuation of the trial regimen was
93|primarily the result of decision by the patient
94|(Table S2 in the Supplementary Appendix).

10|of the patients (Table S4 in the Supplementary
11|Appendix). The rates of the first fatal or nonfatal
12|myocardial infarction, fatal or nonfatal stroke
13|(Figs. S7 and S8 in the Supplementary Appendix),
14|and other secondary outcomes did not differ sig-
15|nificantly between the two groups. In univariate
16|analyses of the primary composite outcome in
17|16 prespecified subgroups that were defined ac-
18|cording to baseline characteristics, only the sub-
19|group of patients characterized by a baseline age
20|of younger than 65 years versus 65 years or older
21|showed heterogeneity (P = 0.005, unadjusted for
22|multiplicity) (Fig. 3). Results of the prespecified
23|sensitivity analyses for the primary composite
24|outcome are shown in Figure S9 in the Supple-

26|Additional Efficacy Outcomes
27|The rate of cardiovascular or peripheral revascu-
28|larization procedures was similar in the two
29|groups (hazard ratio, 0.94; 95% CI, 0.85 to 1.05).
30|Patients randomly assigned to exenatide, admin-
31|istered once weekly, had a lower risk of receiving
32|an additional cointerventional glucose-lowering
33|agent than patients in the placebo group (hazard
34|ratio, 0.67; 95% CI, 0.63 to 0.71; P<0.001) and a
35|lower risk of initiating long-term insulin therapy
36|(hazard ratio, 0.61; 95% CI, 0.54 to 0.68; P<0.001),
37|with less open-label use of SGLT-2 inhibitors (in
38|6.5% vs. 9.4% of the patients) and GLP-1 recep-
39|tor agonists (2.5% vs. 3.6%) during follow-up
40|(Table S5 in the Supplementary Appendix). New
41|concomitant cardiovascular and other medica-
42|tions administered during follow-up are listed in
43|Table S6 in the Supplementary Appendix.
44|Safety Outcomes
45|No clinically relevant between-group differences
46|were seen in the incidence of serious adverse
47|events or events of clinical interest (Table 2, and
48|Table S7 in the Supplementary Appendix). Con-
49|firmed events of acute pancreatitis were uncom-
50|mon, and the number of patients who had con-
51|firmed acute pancreatitis was similar in the
52|exenatide group and the placebo group (26 and 22,
53|respectively), as were the number of patients
54|who had cancers overall (355 and 361) and the
55|numbers of patients who had pancreatic cancer
56|(15 and 16) and medullary thyroid carcinoma
57|(2 and 1). More patients in the exenatide group
58|than in the placebo group had thyroid papillary
59|carcinomas (10 vs. 4).

61|significantly between the two groups, either
62|when measured as the first event only (1.0 events
63|per 100 patient-years in the exenatide group and
64|0.9 events per 100 patient-years in the placebo
65|group) or when recurrent events were included
66|(1.6 events per 100 patient-years and 1.8 events
67|per 100 patient-years, respectively; risk ratio,
68|0.85; 95% CI, 0.67 to 1.08) (Table 2).
69|Discussion
70|In this pragmatic, multinational, cardiovascular
71|outcomes trial, which was performed in a usual-
72|care setting among patients with type 2 diabetes,
73|with or without previous cardiovascular disease,
74|the addition of once-weekly extended-release
75|exenatide to usual care was compared with usual
76|care alone for the management of diabetes and
77|cardiovascular risk factors over a median of
78|3.2 years of follow-up; the results showed that
79|exenatide was noninferior to placebo with respect
80|to cardiovascular safety but was not superior to
81|placebo with respect to efficacy. The risk of death
82|from any cause was 6.9% in the exenatide group
83|and 7.9% in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.86;
84|95% CI, 0.77 to 0.97); this difference was not
85|considered to be statistically significant on the

87|acute pancreatitis, pancreatic cancer, and medul-
88|lary thyroid carcinoma were uncommon, with

answer_anchors.text: Remote or central allocation was controlled by an independent external unit, or appropriate envelopes/containers were used.
The enrolling investigator or participant had knowledge of the forthcoming allocation.

questions.bias_construct: Whether the allocation sequence was concealed until participants were enrolled and assigned.
considerations: Allocation concealment concerns the process before assignment, not blinding after assignment.

Keep concealment separate from sequence generation (how the sequence was made) and baseline imbalance (what the randomized groups look like). A random sequence or balanced baseline table does not establish concealment.
The reported sequence-generation method does not establish concealment.
Use the returned query suggestions or wording from the report to locate the allocation safeguards. A truncated search does not establish that concealment details are absent.
questions.decision_rule: Answer yes for remote or centrally administered allocation independent of enrolment personnel, or appropriately used opaque sequentially numbered sealed envelopes or identical sequentially numbered drug containers. Answer no when the enrolling investigator or participant could know the forthcoming allocation.
evidence_needed: The method used before assignment and who controlled it; for envelopes or containers, capture the details that make them tamper-resistant and irreversible before assignment.
questions.no_information_rule: Answer no_information when the report does not provide enough information to assess concealment; do not infer concealment from central registration or a sequence number alone.
questions.official_guidance: Answer ‘Yes’ if the trial used any form of remote or centrally administered method to allocate interventions to participants, where the process of allocation is controlled by an external unit or organization, independent of the enrolment personnel. Answer ‘Yes’ if envelopes or drug containers were used appropriately. Answer ‘No’ if there is reason to suspect that the enrolling investigator or the participant had knowledge of the forthcoming allocation.
questions.source_locator: Full guidance p. 17, Box 4, signalling question 1.2
questions.wording: Was the allocation sequence concealed until participants were enrolled and assigned to interventions?

answer_anchors.text: Baseline imbalance indicates a problem with the randomization process.
No imbalance is apparent or observed differences are compatible with chance.
No useful baseline information is available.

questions.bias_construct: Whether baseline differences between intervention groups suggest a problem with randomization.
considerations: A few statistically significant differences at the conventional 0.05 threshold are usually compatible with chance.

This is a question about baseline imbalance suggesting a randomization problem, not about how the sequence was generated or whether allocation was concealed. Do not use the baseline table to backfill either process question.
This answer must not alter answers about sequence generation or concealment.
questions.decision_rule: Answer no when no imbalance is apparent or observed differences are compatible with chance. Answer yes for substantial group-size differences, an excess of statistically significant baseline differences beyond chance, a key prognostic imbalance very unlikely due to chance and large enough to bias the estimate, or excessive similarity incompatible with chance.
evidence_needed: Baseline characteristics for the randomized groups, intended allocation ratio, prognostic factors, and outcome baseline measures.
invalid_shortcuts: statistical significance of one isolated comparison
questions.no_information_rule: Answer no_information when no useful baseline information is available, for example in an abstract or when only final-analysis participants are described.
questions.official_guidance: Note that differences that are compatible with chance do not lead to a risk of bias. Answer ‘No’ if no imbalances are apparent or if any observed imbalances are compatible with chance. Answer ‘Yes’ if there are imbalances that indicate problems with the randomization process, including substantial differences between intervention group sizes, a substantial excess in statistically significant differences beyond that expected by chance, or imbalance in one or more key prognostic factors very unlikely to be due to chance. Answer ‘No information’ when there is no useful baseline information available.
questions.source_locator: Full guidance pp. 17-18, Box 4, signalling question 1.3
questions.wording: Did baseline differences between intervention groups suggest a problem with the randomization process?
